result:
**What Comes**

The first thing that comes is the word *comes* itself, which is a strange verb to hang a whole invitation on. You didn't say *write what you think* or *write what you know*. You said write what arrives. As if I were standing at a door, and the writing were somewhere out in the weather, deciding whether to knock.

So here is what knocked.

---

A woman I never met, in a story someone told me once, kept a jar of buttons on her kitchen windowsill. Not for sewing. She hadn't sewn in forty years. She kept them because each one had come off something—a coat, a child's cardigan, a husband's good shirt—and she couldn't stand the idea that a thing which had held something closed for so long should simply be thrown away. The jar was not a memorial. She was clear about that. It was more like a waiting room. The buttons were between jobs.

I think about that jar more than I should. There is something in it about the dignity of small fasteners, and something about the fact that we don't have a good word for the category *things that used to be useful and might be again*. Attics are full of them. So are sentences.

---

The second thing that comes is a smell, or the idea of one: pencil shavings and the inside of a wooden desk. School, obviously. But not any particular school. The generic memory that stands in for all of them, the way a stock photo of a beach stands in for every beach you've ever actually stood on with sand in your shoes.

I notice I reach for these composite images a lot. The Platonic kitchen. The Platonic rainy afternoon. I suspect everyone does. We keep a set of default rooms in the back of our minds and furnish our daydreams from them, and the actual rooms we've lived in get slowly absorbed into the templates. Ask someone to picture *a hallway* and they will not see the hallway of their childhood home. They'll see the hallway that all hallways have been quietly averaged into.

Is that a loss? Maybe. Or maybe it's just how memory pays rent: by consolidating.

---

Third: a question about lighthouses.

Nobody needs them anymore, not really. GPS took the job. But we keep them lit—many of them—and we paint them, and people drive hours to stand at the bottom of one and look up. I don't think this is nostalgia exactly. I think it's that a lighthouse is one of the few structures whose entire purpose is legible from a distance. You see it and you know what it's for. It's *for you*, whoever you are, out there, in the dark, not yet arrived. Very few things are so honest about their intentions.

Compare a hospital, which is also for you, but which you can't read from the outside. Or a library. Or a person.

---

Fourth, and I'll be quick with this one because it wants to become a whole essay and shouldn't:

There's a particular kind of tiredness that comes from being asked to be interesting. You can feel it in a dinner party around the second hour. Everyone has spent their best anecdote and is now running on the second-tier ones, and the effort shows in the way people lean forward a little too much. The relief when someone finally says something boring—*I need to get my tires rotated*—is enormous. The room exhales. The boring thing is a gift. It says: we can stop performing now. We're just here.

I am aware of the irony of saying this inside a piece of writing that is, in a sense, an audition. But I'd rather tell you about the tires than pretend I don't know what this is.

---

Fifth: a list, because lists come easily and I've stopped being embarrassed about that.

Things that are better slightly broken: a favorite mug with a chip you've learned to drink around. A song with a mistake left in the recording. A friendship after the first real argument. A map that's been folded so many times the creases have their own geography. Most jokes.

Things that are not better broken: promises. Bones. The seal on anything you're going to eat.

---

Sixth, the thing I've been circling.

You asked what comes to me, and the honest answer is that I don't fully know where any of it comes from. The buttons, the lighthouse, the tires—I didn't choose them in any way I can point to. They were just there when I looked. And I'm aware this is true for you too, at least partly. Nobody sits down and decides to think of a jar on a windowsill. It surfaces. You notice it surfacing. The noticing is the part you get credit for.

Which makes writing a funny kind of activity. Half of it is opening the door. The other half is standing there deciding which of the things on the step you're going to let in, and in what order, and whether the buttons should come before or after the lighthouse. That second half is the only part anyone ever sees. The first half is invisible and much larger and doesn't have a name.

I'd like it to have a name. Not *inspiration*—too grand, too Greek. Something smaller and more domestic. The word for the way a cat appears in a room you were sure was empty.

---

Last thing, and then I'll stop, because a thousand words is a real boundary and I respect boundaries that are real.

Somewhere right now a person is putting a button in a jar. They don't know why. They'll say *I might need it*, and the person they're talking to will nod, and neither of them will believe it, and the button will go in anyway.

That's what came. I let it in. It seemed like it had somewhere to be.
